client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I keep trying to focus at work, but these memories of her just flood in out of nowhere — her voice, things she used to say, moments we shared — and I completely lose track of what I'm doing. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because nothing is going to bring her back anyway.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds incredibly heavy, and I want you to know that the memories flooding in — her voice, those moments — are a sign of how deeply you loved her, not something broken in you. I also noticed something as you were speaking: your words described the struggle, but your voice carried something quieter, almost like a kind of exhaustion or resignation underneath it all. I'm curious — when you say talking won't help because nothing brings her back, does it feel more like hopelessness, or is there a part of you that's also just very, very tired of hurting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's both, honestly. I'm exhausted from waking up every morning and having that split second where I forget she's gone, and then it hits me all over again. And yeah, maybe there's some hopelessness in there too, because no matter how many times I talk about it, she's still not here when I go home.
therapist: That moment you're describing — that split second of forgetting — sounds like one of the cruelest parts of grief, and the exhaustion of living through it repeatedly every single morning makes so much sense. As you spoke just now, your voice felt softer and quieter than the weight of what you were describing, almost like part of you has gone a little still inside, maybe even numb from carrying this. I wonder — underneath the exhaustion and the hopelessness, is there also something like loneliness in it, like you're grieving not just her absence but also the version of your day that used to include her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... I think that's right, actually. It's not just that she's gone, it's that my whole day used to be built around her — feeding her in the morning, coming home knowing she'd be there, that kind of thing. And now there's just this silence where all of that used to be, and I don't really know who I am in a day that doesn't have her in it anymore.
therapist: What you just described — not knowing who you are in a day without her — that's such a profound and honest thing to name, and it takes real courage to sit with that question rather than push it away. The rhythm of caring for her wasn't just routine, it was part of how you understood yourself, and losing that is its own kind of loss layered on top of losing her. I'm wondering, when you imagine a morning that might one day feel okay again, even just a little — does any part of you have a sense of what that could look like, or does it still feel too far away to picture?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I honestly can't picture it yet — every time I try, I just feel this wave of guilt, like imagining a "good morning" without her is somehow a betrayal. It's like my brain won't let me go there, because if I can picture being okay, then maybe I didn't need her as much as I thought, or maybe losing her wasn't as devastating as it feels. I know that probably doesn't make logical sense, but that's what comes up when I try to imagine it.
therapist: That guilt you're describing actually makes a lot of sense — your mind has created a kind of loyalty test, where staying in pain feels like proof of how much she mattered to you. But I want to gently offer another way to look at it: imagining a morning that feels okay someday isn't a betrayal of her, it's actually a reflection of how deeply she shaped you — because the person who could find peace again would still be someone she loved and raised. I'm curious, do you think she would have wanted that guilt for you, or is there a part of you that already knows what she would have said about it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're probably right about what she would have wanted. She always used to tell me to stop being so hard on myself, so yeah, I think she'd be frustrated seeing me like this. But it still feels like... if I let myself be okay, I'm somehow closing a door on her, and I'm not ready for that door to close.
therapist: The image of a door is such a meaningful one, and I want to reflect something back to you — what if staying connected to her doesn't require that door to stay open through pain, but could instead live in you, in the way she shaped how you love, how you care, how you're even sitting here trying to understand yourself right now? She already told you who she wanted you to be when she said "stop being so hard on yourself," and carrying that forward might actually be one of the most alive ways to keep her with you. What do you think she meant when she said that to you — was it something she said often, and did it ever land for you in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's... a lot to sit with. She did say it often, usually when I'd spiral after making some small mistake, and honestly in those moments it mostly just frustrated me — like, easy for you to say, you know? But hearing it now, the way you framed it, I don't know, it feels different, like maybe she was trying to give me something I kept refusing to take.
therapist: What you just said — that she was trying to give you something you kept refusing to take — that's a really significant moment of insight, and it sounds like something is shifting a little inside you right now as you sit with it. It's almost like grief is offering you a second chance to receive what she was always trying to give, even if you couldn't quite accept it when she was here. I wonder, now that you're hearing it differently, what it might feel like to actually take it — to let her voice be the one that quiets the harshness you turn on yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Like, the idea of letting her voice be the one I hear instead of all that harsh criticism I pile on myself... it sounds beautiful, but it also feels almost impossible, because I've been listening to that critical voice for so long it feels like it's just part of me. I'm not sure I even know how to let something gentler in without it feeling fake or like I'm just making it up.
therapist: The fact that it feels impossible doesn't mean it is — it means that critical voice has had a lot of practice, and gentler ones are just newer and less worn-in, not fake. What you described as "making it up" is actually what change feels like at first, because you're building a new path that doesn't have years of use behind it yet. I'm curious — can you remember even one small moment, maybe recently or from long ago, where you heard her voice in your head and it actually softened something in you, even just for a second?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... maybe. There was this one time a few weeks ago when I was spiraling pretty bad at like two in the morning, just convinced I was a terrible friend for canceling plans, and I heard her say something like "you were exhausted, you needed rest." I think it did slow things down for a second, but then the other voice just came back louder and I figured I'd basically just talked myself into an excuse.
therapist: What you just described is actually really important — her voice *did* come through, and it *did* slow things down, even if only for a moment, and that's not nothing. But I notice the way you told that story, you almost immediately took that moment away from yourself by reframing it as "just making up an excuse," which sounds a lot like that critical voice swooping back in to discredit her. What if "you were exhausted, you needed rest" wasn't an excuse at all — what if it was simply true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... yeah, maybe it was true that I was exhausted. But the second you say that, some part of me just goes, "okay but everyone's exhausted, that doesn't make you special or give you a pass." It's like I can't even let myself have that for more than two seconds before something in me pulls it back.
therapist: That voice that says "everyone's exhausted, that doesn't make you special" — that's a really harsh standard, because by that logic, no one would ever deserve rest or care, including people you love. I'm struck by how quickly and automatically it moves, like it's on guard specifically to make sure you don't get too much relief. I'm wondering — if a close friend said to you "I canceled plans because I was exhausted," would you really turn to them and say "so what, everyone's exhausted, that doesn't give you a pass"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: No, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them to rest and that it's okay. But it feels different when it's me — like I'm supposed to be held to a stricter standard for some reason, and I don't even fully know why I believe that.
therapist: The fact that you don't fully know why you hold yourself to that stricter standard is actually one of the most important things you've said today, because it suggests it's not a conscious choice — it's something you absorbed somewhere along the way, and that means it can be questioned. And I notice as you said that, your voice went quite soft, almost like there's something tender or uncertain underneath the words, like part of you is genuinely puzzled by yourself in a way that feels a little vulnerable. That gap — between how you'd treat a friend and how you treat yourself — that's exactly the space where your grandmother's voice was trying to reach you all along, and I think it's worth us exploring where that stricter standard came from.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
